title: How the Placebo Effect Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the placebo effect: the etymology of "placebo" (hired mourners, "I shall please"), early history from the 1700s-1800s (Thomas Jefferson's "Pious Fraud," John Haygarth), Henry Beecher's WWII saline observation and the double-blind placebo trial, and the 1955 Beecher finding of about 35 percent response. They discuss expectancy effects, classical conditioning, brain imaging studies (UCLA EEG antidepressant study), endorphin and dopamine links, and the nocebo effect. They cover Ted Kaptchuk's research on ritual and the placebo response, doctors prescribing placebos and AMA guidance, criticisms of placebo research, and obacalp, a children's placebo product. The episode ends with a listener mail from Alex in Perth, Western Australia, thanking the show staff.

segments.title: Opening banter and origin of the word placebo
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then trace the word placebo to 14th-century hired mourners and its Latin meaning 'I shall please.'

segments.title: Ted Kaptchuk and early placebo research
segments.summary: Introduces Ted Kaptchuk, a former acupuncturist turned Harvard researcher, and his criticism over control groups in a 2001 New England Journal of Medicine critique. Explains the need for placebo and no-treatment groups and double-blind design.

segments.title: History of placebos and Henry Beecher
segments.summary: Covers Henry Beecher's WWII saline observation, the 1775 placebo definition, Thomas Jefferson's 1807 'Pious Fraud' remark, John Haygarth's early studies, and Beecher's 1955 finding of about 35 percent response.

segments.title: Doctors prescribing placebos
segments.summary: Discusses doctors who prescribe placebos, often without telling patients, and why they might do so.

segments.title: Defining placebo and placebo effect
segments.summary: Defines the placebo as the inert treatment and the placebo effect as the real improvement; notes placebos can be injections, fake surgery, vitamins, or sugar pills. Mentions that color, shape, and size of pills affect responses, and blue and red pills' reputed effects.

segments.title: Mechanisms: expectancy, conditioning, brain studies, endorphins and dopamine
segments.summary: Explains subject and observer expectancy effects, classical conditioning, a UCLA study on antidepressant placebo brain activity via EEG, a 1970s dental study on endorphin blocking, a University of Michigan endorphin study, and dopamine and genetic predisposition.

segments.title: Nocebo effect
segments.summary: Describes the nocebo effect, where placebo takers experience side effects, with chemotherapy-related nausea as an example of conditioning.

segments.title: Ritual, personal anecdote, and expectation in treatment
segments.summary: Kaptchuk's view that ritual, such as bedside manner, perceived cost and effectiveness, drives placebo response, with his 'schmaltzy' care study. Hosts share an anecdote about an emergency room visit and being called a hypochondriac. Notes that telling patients a drug is a painkiller changes results, and a jaw pain study with saline.

segments.title: Criticisms and ethics of placebo use
segments.summary: Covers criticisms that placebo effect may reflect hypochondria or natural recovery, surveys of doctors prescribing placebos (University of Chicago 2007, 2008 survey of 600 doctors), the AMA 2006 guideline, and open-label placebo ideas.

segments.title: Obacalp children's placebo
segments.summary: Discusses obacalp, a placebo marketed for children and invented by Jin Boutner in 2008, with debate about teaching kids about pills. Hosts recall children's orange aspirin and a golf-themed Caddyshack aside.

segments.title: Listener mail from Alex in Perth
segments.summary: Hosts thank staff including Rebecca, Sherry, and Joe. Listener Alex from Perth, Western Australia, writes about finding the show during a job search and thanks the hosts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact details for social media, email, and the website.
